Anand sat on the stool in Salma's tailoring shop in the bazaar while she pinned a hem. Instead of talking about himself he asked, "How did you start this shop?"
Salma laughed. "Nobody asks that." She had begun with one borrowed machine in her father's storeroom, she said, sewing school uniforms at night after her shifts at the ginning mill.
"Weren't you scared?"
"Terrified. My brothers said a woman can't run a shop." She bit off a thread.
"And what did you do?"
"Ran it."
Anand didn't say "you should have" or offer advice. He nodded and asked how she'd taught her first apprentice. Salma pulled up a second stool. "Sit properly. This will take a while."

qa.a: Salma began with one borrowed machine in her father's storeroom.

I sat in on the packing team's weekly meeting. They have used the same handover sheet for six years and are proud of their low error rate. Varun, the longest-serving member, said, "We've always done it this way, and it works." Two newer members looked at their phones.

Then someone mentioned that a supplier had quietly moved to a competitor last year. I asked them to list three things a new person might find odd about our process. They wrote seven.

qa.a: It let the team see the process through a newcomer's eyes, and they wrote seven items, showing they had more to notice than they had said.

qa.a: Varun was probably defensive or uneasy at first, having said the way works, but the list may have shown that the pride was justified in part and open to improvement.
